summary: Looks at how to make TCP work well for all users, including those on long thin networks, which have high delay and low bandwidth. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Some links are like a very long skinny straw. This explains how to make the Internet work smoothly even through one.

questions: what is a long thin network
how to optimize tcp for wireless
why is latency bad for tcp
subtitle: How to make TCP work well on wireless networks with high latency and low bandwidth.

tldr.problem: TCP was designed for wired networks, but wireless WANs (W-WANs) have high latency and low bandwidth, causing TCP to adapt slowly and perform poorly. TCP's mechanisms break down or become inefficient over such links.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2757 reviews existing proposals and recommends a set of TCP optimizations including larger initial windows, header compression, selective acknowledgements, and SNOOP protocol at intermediate nodes, with each mechanism chosen to be safe in non-wireless environments too.
tldr.outcome: These optimizations allow TCP to operate more efficiently over long thin networks without destabilizing the Internet. Many recommendations have been adopted in practice, though some remain experimental.

today: RFC 2757 is informational. The recommended optimizations have been partially adopted in mobile networks and modern TCP implementations, though the RFC notes that not all recommendations became standards. Header compression, larger initial windows, and selective acknowledgements are widely implemented. The SNOOP protocol is used in some systems but has not become universal.

sections.title: Introduction: Long Thin Networks
sections.content:
A long thin network (LTN) is a wireless wide-area network with two key problems: high round-trip latency and low bandwidth. For example, a W-WAN might have 500 milliseconds of round-trip delay and only 24 Kbps of bandwidth, while traditional networks have 3 ms latency and 1.5 Mbps. This long-latency, low-bandwidth combination is called a "thin pipe."

The delay matters because it determines how long the sender must wait for acknowledgements. The bandwidth matters because it limits how much data fits in the "pipe" at any moment. TCP's congestion control relies on feedback from the receiver, but this feedback takes a very long time to arrive over an LTN, making the protocol adapt slowly.
sections.eli5: Imagine drinking from a very long, narrow straw. Not only is it hard for liquid to flow, but you cannot tell if the liquid is coming until a long time after you start sucking. That makes it hard for you to adjust your effort.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Problem Characteristics
sections.content:
The typical LTN topology includes a wireless mobile device connected via a wireless link to an intermediate node (base station), which then connects to the wired Internet. The RFC assumes the wireless link is the last hop and that a single intermediate node sees all traffic between the mobile device and external servers.

Wireless links have several distinctive problems: burst errors from radio interference, variable latency from retransmissions and handoffs, and in some cases disconnections when signal is lost. These characteristics differ from wired networks, where loss is usually a sign of congestion, not corruption. TCP misinterprets corruption loss as congestion and unnecessarily reduces its transmission rate.
sections.eli5: The mobile device talks to a base station, which talks to the rest of the world. The wireless part can have hiccups and dropouts. When packets get corrupted by radio interference, TCP wrongly thinks the network is too crowded.

sections.title: Why Standard TCP Performs Poorly
sections.content:
TCP uses slow start to probe the network: it starts by sending one segment and doubles the window each time it receives acknowledgements. This is safe but very slow over long-latency networks. Because the round-trip time is long, feedback arrives slowly, so the window grows slowly. If the initial window is only one segment and RTT is 500 ms, the sender sits idle 500 ms per segment at the start of each connection.

Additionally, duplicate acknowledgements trigger fast retransmit, which assumes that lost packets indicate congestion. On wireless links with high error rates, this causes unnecessary window reductions. Delayed acknowledgements compound the problem: the receiver waits for more data before sending an ACK, further delaying the sender's feedback loop.
sections.eli5: TCP starts by sending one piece. When the sender hears back (after a long wait), it sends two pieces. After another long wait, four pieces. This doubling is safe but slow. Also, TCP gives up too easily when packets go missing, thinking the network is crowded when it is actually just noisy.

sections.title: Recommended Optimizations
sections.content:
Larger Initial Window: Allow the sender to transmit two segments initially instead of one. This is now in the TCP standard and saves one round-trip time on short connections.

Header Compression: Compress TCP and IP headers to reduce overhead. Van Jacobson (VJ) header compression is widely deployed. IP Header Compression (IPHC) is also recommended and is more robust to packet loss.

Selective Acknowledgements (SACK): Receivers tell the sender which segments arrived, not just the highest sequence number. This helps recover from burst errors more efficiently.

SNOOP Protocol: An intermediate node on the wireless link can locally retransmit lost packets and suppress duplicate acknowledgements to the sender. This prevents unnecessary congestion window reductions and improves throughput.

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN): Networks mark packets (instead of dropping them) when congested. Receivers tell the sender about these marks, so the sender reduces its window only when the network is truly congested, not when corruption causes loss.

The RFC recommends against T/TCP and split-TCP approaches that significantly alter TCP semantics. Application-level proxies are conditionally recommended if the user can control their use.
sections.eli5: Send two pieces at the start, not one. Squeeze the headers smaller. Receiver tells the sender exactly which pieces arrived. The base station can fix lost pieces locally instead of making the sender retransmit. The network can say "I am getting crowded" instead of silently dropping packets.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many of the recommended mechanisms have been implemented. Larger initial windows and fast retransmit are standard. Header compression is widely used in mobile networks. SNOOP has been studied extensively, though it does not work if traffic is encrypted with IPsec, because the intermediate node cannot examine the TCP headers.

A key constraint is that legacy servers cannot be modified. This means solutions must work at the mobile device or intermediate node (or both), without changing the servers. This rules out mechanisms that require bidirectional changes.

Security concerns arise when intermediate nodes perform optimizations: SNOOP and header compression require examining and modifying IP packets, which conflicts with end-to-end encryption. Users who prioritize security should use application-level protection (SSL, SOCKS) instead.
sections.eli5: These tricks are being used on real wireless networks. The main challenge is that the base station cannot help if messages are locked with encryption, because it cannot see inside them. Users who need privacy should lock their messages end-to-end instead of relying on the wireless link.
